solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Enjoyed Subaru's edgeways cornering

indicators.note: the run of words is cornered around the letters, so they sit concealed inside 'Subaru's edgeways'

explanation.surface: A driver relishes taking bends sideways in a Subaru.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cornering' looks like motoring talk but means the clue words hold the letters: they span the end of 'Subaru's' and the start of 'edgeways'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have used something is to have had the benefit of it, as in enjoying a privilege.

clue.text: Thingamy's activities

definitions.meaning: a vague word for an object whose name escapes you, a whatsit
the things someone gets up to, their goings-on

explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun means both a whatsit (colloquial British) and a person's goings-on or deeds.

clue.text: Self-styled popular celebrity on left's unknown

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a name is a famous person, as in 'a big name'
Y is one of the algebraic unknowns, like x and z

explanation.surface: A self-proclaimed celebrity of the political left turns out to be a nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nominal only, called so by itself without substance, is merely so-called or self-styled.

clue.text: Issue is degenerate runs away

indicators.note: 'runs away' tells us the runs letter goes away from the word for degenerate

parts.note: to degenerate is to go backwards, to regress
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A complaint that some issue is going downhill and running off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link here. 'away' removes R (runs) from REGRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to issue is to come out or emerge, and an exit or going out is the noun sense matched here: a way out or outflow.

clue.text: To come across undrinkable beer's nothing

parts.note: bum is British slang for bad or worthless, so an undrinkable pint is a bum one
a pint is a measure of beer
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Discovering that the nasty beer is free sounds like a complaint about a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' starts the infinitive and is a link. BUM is British slang for poor quality.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet someone by chance is to encounter them unexpectedly, a phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Unlimited riches that could include mine

indicators.note: unlimited means the word for riches loses its limits, its first and last letters

parts.note: Mammon is the New Testament word for worldly wealth seen as an evil influence

explanation.surface: Boundless wealth that might stretch to owning a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'mine' is not a pit but an explosive device, which counts as munitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammunition, the short informal word, covers explosive devices such as a landmine.

clue.text: Curse articles strewn across motorway

indicators.note: across means the scattered articles are laid over and around the motorway letter
strewn means scattered about, so the articles' letters are rearranged

parts.note: the articles an, a, the and a again supply these letters
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Someone swearing as newspaper pieces blow all over the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strewn' rearranges the articles AN, A, THE, A into ANATHEA; 'across' then sets those letters around M.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is a formal ecclesiastical curse or ban, hence any curse.

clue.text: A small group under canvas drawing together

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

indicators.note: 'under canvas' means within a tent, so the group goes inside it

parts.note: canvas stands for a tent, as in sleeping under canvas
a ring is a group or gang, as in a spy ring

explanation.surface: A little band camping out are getting closer to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: An astringent substance contracts body tissues, literally pulling them together.

clue.text: Cram tool shed and get hacked off

indicators.note: shed means cast off, so the tool is dropped from the word for cram

parts.note: to shoehorn is to cram something into too small a space
a hoe is a garden tool

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs the garden shed and ends up fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' looks like a garden building but is a verb: SHOEHORN sheds HOE. 'and get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorn is the past participle of shear, meaning cut off, as hair or fleece is cut off.

clue.text: Foodies try game rejected by department store

parts.note: to have a go is to try

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the letters for the game are reversed

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
M and S is Marks & Spencer, the British department store chain

explanation.surface: Food lovers sample a game that a big shop has turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: M&S (Marks & Spencer) is a British high-street store; '&' is spelt out as AND. 'by' is a link meaning next to.
explanation.definitionFit: Gourmands are people who love eating, close enough in sense to foodies and gourmets.

clue.text: Dirty fellow (East-ender) tore into food with teeth

parts.note: Dirty Den was Den Watts, the villain of the BBC soap EastEnders

indicators.note: 'East-ender' read as the ending of East gives its last letter

parts.note: someone who tore into food ate it

explanation.surface: A grubby Londoner from the East End wolfs down his dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: '(East-ender)' looks like a description of Den, the EastEnders character, but supplies the last letter of 'East'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dentate is a botanical and zoological term meaning toothed or having tooth-like notches.

clue.text: Dramatist covering end of political conspirator

indicators.note: covering means the dramatist's name wraps around the next letter

parts.note: Dennis Potter was an English television dramatist

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of political

explanation.surface: A playwright writing about a political schemer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plotter is one who plots, a schemer, synonymous with a conspirator.

clue.text: Count Bruce's top basslines — with odd exceptions

indicators.note: top means the first letter of Bruce's
the odd-numbered letters of basslines are excepted, leaving the even ones

explanation.surface: A judgement that a musician's bass lines are good apart from a few odd ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Count Basie was the American jazz bandleader; 'Count' is his title, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Basie was the jazz pianist and bandleader; his stage title alone is a fair pointer.

clue.text: Visibly tired beady leer somehow focused on celebrity's bottom

indicators.note: somehow means in some other way, so the letters of beady leer and the bottom letter are rearranged together
bottom in a down clue is the last letter of celebrity's

explanation.surface: An exhausted onlooker leers at a famous person's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges BEADY LEER together with Y, the last letter of 'celebrity's'; 'focused on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with bleary eyes looks blurred and exhausted, so the phrase means visibly weary.

clue.text: Liberal censures new protection

indicators.note: liberal means free or loose, so the letters of censures are taken freely

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician condemns a new protective measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks like the party but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunscreen is a lotion that guards skin against ultraviolet rays.

clue.text: Judgment time to oust five in assembly

indicators.note: to oust means to replace, so the time letter takes the place of the Roman five

parts.note: a convention is a large assembly or conference

explanation.surface: A verdict that it is time to expel five from a legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'five' is the Roman numeral V.
explanation.definitionFit: A contention is an assertion or opinion argued for, a considered judgment.

clue.text: Less than serious event, for instance, a kind of opera with no pace or dancing

parts.note: G and S, Gilbert and Sullivan, is a kind of comic opera

indicators.note: dancing means moving about, so the letters of no pace or are rearranged

explanation.surface: A frivolous show, say a light opera, lacking any pace or dance.
explanation.walkthrough: G&S is Gilbert and Sullivan, whose comic operettas are a genre of their own; '&' is spelt AND.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg-and-spoon race is a comic novelty race at school sports days, not a serious contest.

clue.text: Tatty dining car neither fashionable nor popular embodying outmoded status symbol

indicators.note: embodying means containing, so the jumbled letters wrap around the next piece
tatty means shabby and disordered, so the remaining letters are jumbled
neither ... nor frames the two things to be left out of dining car
nor marks the second thing to be left out of dining car

parts.note: in means fashionable
in also means popular
old means outmoded, out of date

explanation.surface: A shabby restaurant carriage that is neither trendy nor liked holds an old-fashioned perk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neither ... nor' strips both words meaning 'in' from DINING CAR, leaving DGCAR, which 'Tatty' rearranges as GCARD around the outmoded piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A premium credit card once flaunted as a mark of wealth was a classic status symbol.

clue.text: Substitute securing point for champions

indicators.note: securing means holding, so the substitute word holds the point inside it

parts.note: a standby is a substitute available at short notice
S is south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A reserve player keeps hold of a point for the winners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'champions' is a verb here, meaning supports. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To champion a cause is to back it loyally, to support it through trouble.

clue.text: Contest whose participants must get used to taking stick

definitions.text: Contest whose participants must get used to taking stick

parts.words: Contest whose participants must get used to taking stick
parts.note: taking stick sounds like enduring criticism, but here the stick is a baton handed between team runners

explanation.walkthrough: 'taking stick' is the British idiom for being criticised; here it is literal, the baton passed between team runners.
explanation.definitionFit: In this team track event each runner must take the baton from a teammate.

clue.text: £25 in English money for Guinness, Beck's or Pimm's?

indicators.note: in means the slang sum sits inside the letters for English and money

parts.note: M is the economists' abbreviation for money, as in M1 money supply
pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: A query about what twenty-five quid in English cash buys in the way of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: PONY is British slang for £25. Each drink is named after its founder, so each is an example, hence '?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Each drink brand is named after a person, Arthur Guinness, Heinrich Beck and James Pimm, making them examples of name-derived terms.

clue.text: Forster bumped into tourist in Cornwall

parts.note: E. M. Forster, the novelist, gives his initials
met means encountered or bumped into

explanation.surface: The novelist Forster encountered a holidaymaker in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cornish dialect the word, literally an ant, is a mildly scornful term for a visitor; Cornwall is a holiday county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornish locals use this dialect word for an ant to describe visiting tourists swarming in summer.

clue.text: See 26
Left around 100 worked up

indicators.note: around means the word for left goes round the number

parts.note: exited means went out, left
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: Someone went out about a hundred times and got agitated.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agitated or stirred up emotionally is to be thrilled or aroused, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Hit hard — lump coming up

indicators.note: coming up in a down clue means the word for lump is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a knot is a lump, as in a knot in wood or muscle

explanation.surface: A blow strikes hard and a bump starts to swell.
explanation.walkthrough: This is British slang, mostly from cricket, for striking the ball forcefully.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonk is informal British slang for hitting a ball or person with force.

clue.text: Speaking about conditions?

parts.note: on means about, as in a talk on art
terms are conditions or stipulations of an agreement

explanation.surface: A question about the wording of contract stipulations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaking' is not talk but being on friendly relations, as in 'are you two speaking?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people still speaking are friendly, on good relations with each other.

clue.text: Pain mixed with pleasure meeting resistance after a time by home bird

parts.note: S and M, sadomasochism, mixes pain with pleasure
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance
in means at home

explanation.surface: A kinky scene with a time and a home sounds like a racy tabloid tale.
explanation.walkthrough: S&M (sadomasochism) is spelt S AND M; 'meeting', 'after' and 'by' are link words joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: This small brown member of the swallow family nests in burrows in riverbanks.

clue.text: England and Hodgson claiming funky music may be sort that carries a message

indicators.note: claiming means taking hold of, so the manager's forename holds the music inside

parts.note: Roy Hodgson was the England football manager when this puzzle appeared
R and B is rhythm and blues, a funky style of music

explanation.surface: The England football manager taking up funk might be someone with a message to send.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' and 'may be' are link words; R&B is spelt R AND B.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy employed to run small errands typically delivers notes and messages.

clue.text: Stars love return of classic Hollywood genre

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: return of means the genre's name is turned back to front

parts.note: film noir is a classic Hollywood genre of dark crime dramas

explanation.surface: Film stars adore a revival of old Hollywood crime films.
explanation.definitionFit: Orion is a prominent winter constellation, a named group of stars.
